findings.where: Screen 11 (Fresh batches) text and read, and screen 13 (A long tail) puzzle and why
findings.what: The leaning insulation-resistance pile on screen 13 (mean 212.5 MΩ, SD 79.4 MΩ) holds 34, 48 and 49 of its 50 readings within 1, 2 and 3 SD. That is 68%, 96% and 98%, the same as the bell batch's 33, 48 and 49. So 'Those have different shares' is untrue for the very pile it names, and the puzzle asks about the one share, 95% within 2 SD, that this lean does not change. Teach what the lean does change, which the pile shows. Both readings beyond 2 SD, at 378 and 455 MΩ, sit on the high side and none on the low side. So screen 12's 'half on each side' fails, and a far-high reading is far less rare than the bell says. Ask the puzzle about that, for example 'about what share land above the mean + 2 SD?', and let the right answer draw the band so the lopsided count shows.

findings.where: Screen 5 (The ruler) and screen 9 (Far out on the ruler), the 'Ringed reading' tile
findings.what: The tile reads a bare '+2.0' with no unit, right under a slider reading '+0.6 V', so it can be taken for volts. K.readout drops `unit` whenever `fmt` is given (kit.js: `if (o.unit && !o.fmt)`), so the declared unit 'SD' never shows. Give the unit without a custom fmt, or name it in the label, such as 'Ringed reading, in SDs'.

The honest reading picked to land past the upper limit, 115.9 V, sits 3.0 SD from the batch's mean. On screen 3 it is the one bead left outside the 99.7% band (49 of 50). By the lesson's own ruler, the mean and SD of the other 49, it sits 3.37 SD out, past the 3.3 SD 'outlier' line. Yet screen 9 says a reading that far out is 'very rare by chance' and 'more likely a slip', and screen 7 calls this one honest. Pick an opening batch whose honest reading out sits between 2.7 and 3 SD (dataviz.md's prototype seed sits at +2.9 SD). Or say it on screen 9: an honest reading lands past 3 SD now and then, as the farthest bead here did, which is why you test again rather than delete.

The brief promised that this lesson introduces a probability as a share of the time, running from 0 to 1, because lesson 5 multiplies reliabilities and takes 1 − p. The lesson says only 'A share of the time is a chance' and never uses the word probability or the 0-to-1 scale. Add a sentence such as 'That chance is the probability, 0.95 written as a number from 0 to 1.'

Dan is sent to drop fresh batches, but no sentence says what the tally should teach. Close it in one sentence, named as this simulation's figure: by script, about one batch in five (0.18) of fifty honest readings has one past limits 2.7 SD out. The brief allows this, and it lands the surprise it promised: honest readings land out often.

The point comes seventh. Six sentences on how the ruler is built, the mean of the other 49 and why the reading is left out, come before 'subtract the mean, then divide by the SD. That count is the reading's z-score.' Lead with the z-score sentence and the ruler, then give the leave-one-out reason.

In the read-through still, 'The smooth curve traces the skyline, then relaxes into a bell' describes motion that a still cannot show. Give the step a `read` that describes the finished picture, such as 'A smooth curve follows the pile's outline: a bell.'

There are five footnote marks ([^1], [^2] twice, [^3] twice), and two of them, both [^3], sit on the habit 'ask why before you delete it', which is not a value Dan would look up. The bold summary repeats [^3]. Keep [^1] on 95%, [^2] on 99.7% and 3.3 SD, and at most one [^3].

findings.where: Sources 2 and 3 (and lesson i1's third source)
findings.what: Both HELM sources are titled '36 36', so the footnote Dan opens names nothing. Title it 'HELM Workbook 36: Descriptive Statistics', and title source 1 'UKAS LAB 12: The Expression of Uncertainty in Testing'.

The 68% is the only rule figure with no `source`, although research has it (LibreTexts, SECONDARY, quotes.json), and the brief asked for an original source to be found at build time. Attach the source to the number, or a primary one such as the NIST handbook.

'Readings that pile into a bell follow the normal curve' is firmer than the lesson's own 'a model of such a pile'. Write 'are well modelled by the normal curve', in line with the brief's 'often modelled'.

findings.where: Screen 9 (Far out on the ruler), motion
findings.what: The film records no motion at all on this screen (settled 0 s), although its ring and ruler are timed to arrive over 0.55 s, exactly as on screen 5, which films about 1 s of motion. Check that the ring and ruler arrive here rather than appear.

The 26-word opening sentence, 'To land 0.9 V high, 3 SD, a bead needs most of its twelve nudges to push it the same way', carries an apposition mid-sentence. Split it: 'Landing 0.9 V high is 3 SD out. A bead needs most of its twelve nudges to push the same way.'
